title: Your Cross-Functional Commitment Is Only as Good as the Handoff
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), September 4, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller diagnoses a specific failure mode in cross-functional leadership: a leader can be perfectly aligned with an external stakeholder while their own team remains internally siloed, so a carefully negotiated commitment quietly falls apart because no one on the team realized they owned the dropped piece. His central diagnostic claim is that generic exhortations to 'be more collaborative' don't fix this, because the real problem is invisibility — team members see the task from their own seat but not the stakeholder depending on it several steps downstream. Mueller's practical tool is a simplified RACI conversation (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed), which he's careful to note has value not in the matrix itself but in the conversation it forces the team to have about who actually owns what. He also flags a common leadership overcorrection: responding to a dropped commitment by becoming more directive only improves compliance, not genuine cross-functional commitment, unless the leader also reconnects each person's task to the stakeholder who depends on it — turning 'what am I doing for my boss' into 'what does this stakeholder need from my work.' The piece closes with a concrete five-minute pre-commitment ritual (naming the deliverable, stakeholder, responsible party, accountable party, and handoff point, then asking what could cause the team to drop the ball) designed to surface unclear ownership before it becomes a stakeholder disappointment.
points: Mueller's core diagnosis — 'you can become externally aligned while your team remains internally siloed' — names a specific leadership blind spot: a leader's own clarity with a stakeholder is no guarantee the team behind them shares that clarity about who owns what.

His distinction between improving compliance (being more directive) and improving genuine cross-functional commitment (connecting each person's task to the stakeholder who depends on it) offers leaders a sharper diagnostic for why 'just push harder' fixes often don't stick.

The Five-Minute Handoff Check, ending with the deliberately blunt question 'What could cause us to drop the ball?', gives leaders a lightweight, repeatable ritual for surfacing ownership gaps before a commitment leaves the room, rather than after it has already failed.
quotes: Three days later, you discover that one of your team members did not complete an important part of it. The explanation sounds perfectly reasonable: 'I didn't realize I owned that.'
This is one of the hidden challenges of cross-functional leadership: you can become externally aligned while your team remains internally siloed.
What they may not see is the stakeholder depending on their contribution several steps downstream. Telling people to 'be more collaborative' rarely fixes this. You need to make the handoff visible.
The value isn't the matrix itself. The value is the conversation it forces you and your team to have.
if your team still sees the assignment only as something they are doing for you, you have improved compliance without necessarily improving cross-functional commitment.
Ask the person responsible: 'What does this stakeholder need to be able to do with your work?' Now the assignment has a customer.

Then ask one final question: 'What could cause us to drop the ball?' That five-minute conversation can expose unclear ownership, conflicting priorities, missing information, and assumptions before they become stakeholder disappointments.
